Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on surah 20, verse 1:

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Tafsir of Surat Ta-Ha

It is Meccan.

Among the strange reports is a narration on the authority of Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet said: "Allah, exalted is He, recited Surat Ta-Ha and Ya-Sin two thousand years before He created Adam. The angels said: 'Blessed is the nation upon whom this was sent down, blessed are the hearts that carried this, and blessed are the tongues that spoke this.'"

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Ta-Ha﴾. It is related from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that a man recited to him "Ta-ha" with imalah (the inclination of the vowel), and he said: Recite ﴿Ta-Ha﴾. The man said: Does it not mean "trample the earth with your feet"? He said: "This is how the Messenger of Allah recited it to me."

Opinions have differed concerning the meaning of Ta-Ha. It is related from Ibn Abbas that he said: it is in Syriac, meaning "O man." Al-Kalbi transmitted that it means "O man" in the language of the tribe of Akk. The poet said:

(Indeed foolishness, Ta-ha, is from your nature; may Allah not sanctify the spirits of the accursed.)

And another said:

(I called out "Ta-ha" in the battle, but he did not answer, so I feared that he might be an ally of the enemy.)

It is also said that Ta-Ha is a name of the surah, and it is said that it is an oath which Allah swore by.

It is well known that its meaning is "trample the earth with your feet," and this is also transmitted from Ibn Abbas. Its cause was that the Prophet exerted himself greatly in worship, to the point that he would alternate between his two feet, standing on one and raising the other, so Allah, exalted is He, sent down this verse. Some have related that he stood on a single foot.

Among them are those who said: the Ta is from purity (tahara) and the Ha is from guidance (hidaya). So the Ta indicates the purification of his heart from other than Allah, and the Ha indicates the guidance of his heart to Allah.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 2:

And His saying: ﴿We did not send down the Qur'an to you that you should be distressed﴾, meaning: that you should exert yourself and be weary. It is related that when he (ﷺ) strove hard in worship, the polytheists said: "O Muhammad, the Qur'an was only sent down for your misery." So Allah, exalted is He, revealed this verse. Its meaning is: strive, but do not bear all this hardship to the point that you are attributed with wretchedness.

And His words, ﴿except as a reminder to one who fears﴾ — its meaning: "but rather a reminder," i.e., an admonition and a warning for one who fears (yakhsha). Al-khashya (fear/awe) and al-khawf (fear) have the same meaning. Some scholars distinguished between them, saying: al-khashya is fear whose cause is not known, while al-khawf is fear whose cause is known. This view is weak.

Al-Azhari mentioned that the implied construction of the verse is: "We did not send down the Qur'an upon you so that you would suffer; We sent it down only as a reminder for one who fears."

Qur'anic quotations in ﴿ ﴾ are kept with meaning translated.

And His saying: ﴿a revelation﴾ — meaning: it is a revelation (tanzil) sent down from God, ﴿who created the earth and the heavens, the high ones﴾. And "al-'ula" is the plural of "al-'ulya."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 5:

And His saying: ﴿The Most Merciful is established upon the Throne﴾. Know that the senses of istiwa' (establishment, "being level/settled") in the Arabic language are many. It may mean ʿuluw (elevation, being high above), it may mean istiqrar (settling, remaining in place), it may mean istila' (dominion, taking control, after some difficulty), and it may mean iqbal (turning toward, facing).

The position of the People of the Sunnah is that one believes in it without asking how (takyif). They related from Jaʿfar ibn ʿAbd Allah and Bishr al-Khaffaf, who said: "We were with Malik, when a man came to him and asked him about His saying: ﴿The Most Merciful is established upon the Throne﴾: how is He established?" Malik lowered his head for a while, and sweat covered him from the heat (of the question). Then he said: "The how (kayf) is not conceivable, the establishment (istiwa') is unknown, belief in it is obligatory, and asking about it is an innovation (bidʿah). I do not think you are but a misguided person." Then he ordered that the man be taken out.

The people of hadith transmitted from Sufyan al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, al-Layth ibn Saʿd, Sufyan ibn ʿUyayna, and ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Mubarak that they said concerning the ambiguous (mutashabih) verses: "Let them pass as they came."

Some of them said: its interpretation (ta'wil) is belief in it. As for interpreting istiwa' as istiqbal (facing), that is the interpretation of the Mu'tazilah.

Al-Zajjaj, al-Nahhas, and a group of grammarians from the People of the Sunnah mentioned that in the language istiwa' is not called istila' unless the one who is established overcomes another; and this is not permissible for God, exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 6:

The words of the Most High: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth and whatever is between them﴾. That is: He knows what is in the heavens, what is on the earth, and what is between them.

As for His words: ﴿and whatever is beneath the soil﴾, there are several opinions concerning it. One of them is that al-thara (the soil, earth) is the seventh earth, and another is that al-thara is moist soil, and this is well known in the Arabic language.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr related from Ibn 'Abbas that the earths are upon the back of a fish, the fish is upon the sea, the sea is upon a rock, the rock is upon the horn of a bull, the bull is upon al-thara, and what is beneath al-thara, none knows it but Allah.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 7:

The words of the Most High: ﴿And if you speak aloud, then indeed He knows the secret and what is yet more hidden.﴾ Its meaning: whether you speak aloud or keep it secret, nothing escapes His knowledge. Scholars differed regarding His words ﴿and what is yet more hidden﴾. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "The secret (al-sirr) is what another person speaks to you about, and what is more hidden is what you speak to yourself about." In the verse there is an implied element, and its meaning is: "and what is more hidden than it," that is, more hidden than the secret.

The second view: the "secret" is what you speak to yourself about, and "what is more hidden" is what God Most High casts into your heart afterwards, which you have not spoken to yourself about.

The third view: the secret is the resolve (ʿazima), and what is more hidden is what falls below resolve, as when a thought passes over the heart and you have not resolved upon it.

The fourth view: ﴿He knows the secret and what is yet more hidden﴾ means "and the hidden," that is, the concealed. A poet said:

(Men wish that I would die, and if I die, / Then that is a path in which you are not unique.)

That is, "not the one alone" (bi-l-wahid).

The fifth view: ﴿He knows the secret and what is yet more hidden﴾ means that He concealed His secret from His servants, and this is the view of Ibn Zayd.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 8:

The words of the Most High: ﴿Allah, there is no god but Him. To Him belong the most beautiful names.﴾ It has been said: there is an ellipsis (idmar) in it, and its meaning is: "So call upon Allah by them." And he said: "al-Husna" as an adjective for "al-asma'" (the names) is a plural form, while "al-Husna" is the feminine singular form of the adjective. This is because "hadhihi" (these) encompasses "al-asma'" since it is a plural, just as the feminine singular is used for the feminine plurals. One says: "hadhihi asma'" (these are names). Therefore it is valid to say "husna" and it was not said "husan," and likewise the words of the Most High: ﴿other uses﴾ and it was not said "akhar" (other, masculine).
Almighty Allah's words: ﴿Has there come to you the story of Moses?﴾ Its meaning is: Indeed the story of Moses has come to you. It is an interrogative used in the sense of confirmation (taqrir).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 10:

And His saying: ﴿When he saw a fire﴾. In the narrative: Moses, peace be upon him, was a man of jealous nature (ghayur). He would accompany the caravan at night and withdraw from them during the day, so that his wife would not be seen. Once he lost his way, as was in the knowledge of God the Exalted, and it was a dark night. He saw a fire from afar, ﴿so he said to his family, "Stay here"﴾, that is: remain (aqimu) in place.

And His saying: ﴿I have perceived a fire﴾, that is: I have seen (absartu) a fire.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Perhaps I may bring you from it a burning brand (qabas)﴾. Qabas: anything that has fire at its head, whether a flame (shu'la) or a wick (fatila).

And His saying: ﴿Or find at the fire guidance (huda)﴾, that is: or find near the fire someone who will guide me and show me the way. It is narrated that when he headed toward the fire, he saw a green tree encircled by the fire, and the fire was as bright as it could be, and the tree was as green as it could be. The light of the fire did not alter the greenness of the tree, nor did the greenness of the tree alter the light of the fire.

It is said that the tree was a grapevine (shajarat al-'inab). It is also said it was a tree of 'awsaj (a thorny shrub), and it was said: of 'uliq (a climbing thorny plant).

In the narrative: Moses took some dry grass and approached the tree, and whenever he drew near the tree, the fire receded from him, and whenever he withdrew, the fire drew near. So he remained standing, bewildered, and he was called: "O Moses!"
"The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿So when he came to it, he was called, "O Moses"﴾. We have already explained this."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 12:

And His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am your Lord﴾. It is narrated that when Musa heard the words ﴿O Musa﴾, he said: "Who is it that speaks to me?" He said: ﴿Indeed, I am your Lord﴾.

If it is asked: How did he recognise the speech of Allah, exalted is He? We say: He heard speech that does not resemble the speech of created beings. It is also narrated that he heard it from all its sides.

And His saying: ﴿So take off your sandals﴾. Scholars differed regarding why he was commanded to take off his sandals. It is narrated from ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "They were made from the skin of a dead donkey," and this is the view of Kaʿb.

The second view is that he was commanded to take them off so that he would touch the valley with his feet. This is the view of Mujāhid. It has also been the custom of the Muslims that they take off their sandals when they reach the Sacred Mosque for Hajj, and they perform the ṭawāf barefoot.

And His saying: ﴿Indeed, you are in the sacred valley﴾, i.e., the purified (al-muqaddas, the purified or sanctified one). The poet said:

(And you are a means of reaching the relatives, a clod of earth... seen from afflictions, I am purified (muqaddas))

i.e., purified.

It has also been said: the meaning of "muqaddas" is "blessed therein."

And His saying: ﴿Ṭuwan﴾. Most of the exegetes say that it is the name of the valley. It has also been said: Ṭuwan means "sanctified twice."

Almighty Allah's words: ﴿And I have chosen you﴾, meaning: I have selected you.

And His words: ﴿So listen to what is revealed﴾, meaning: listen to what is revealed to you.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 14:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity except Me, so worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance﴾. That is: no one deserves worship besides Me.

As for His saying: ﴿and establish prayer for My remembrance﴾, there are several opinions regarding it. The first: so that you remember Me in it. The second: that you remember Me, and this is His saying: "Allah is greatest" (Allahu akbar). The third: establish prayer for My remembrance, meaning: pray when you remember the prayer. This is a well-known view. Hammad ibn Salamah narrated from Qatadah, from Anas, that the Prophet said: "Whoever forgets a prayer, let him pray it when he remembers it, for that is its time," and he recited His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and establish prayer for My remembrance﴾.

The Shaykh al-Imam said: Abu al-Husayn ibn al-Naqqur informed us of this hadith, saying: Abu al-Qasim ibn Hababa informed us, saying: Ibn Bint Mani' related to us, saying: Hudbah related to us, from Hammad ibn Salamah... the hadith. It was recorded by Muslim in his Sahih from Hudbah.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 15:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming—I almost conceal it﴾. Regarding this verse there are several opinions, and it is difficult (mushkilah).

It is narrated from ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud and Ubayy ibn Kaʿb that they both recited: "I almost conceal it from myself." Some have transmitted: "How then should I reveal it to you?" This is one of the opinions concerning the meaning of the verse.

If someone says: How does His saying "I almost conceal it from myself" hold together? We say: This is according to the custom of the Arabs. When the Arabs exaggerate in reporting the concealment of a thing, they say: "I hid it even from myself."

The second opinion: His saying ﴿akaadu﴾ means "I intend" (uridu), and the meaning is: "Indeed, the Hour is coming; I intend to conceal it." This is the view of al-Akhfash.

The third opinion: His saying ﴿akaadu﴾ is superfluous (silah), and the meaning is: "Indeed, the Hour is coming; I conceal it."

The fourth opinion: "Indeed, the Hour is coming, I almost..." and the meaning of akaadu is the approach of occurrence and arrival, as Dabaʾi al-Barjami said:

(I was resolved and did not act; I almost did, and I wish I had left ʿUthman's wives weeping over him.)

So his saying "kadtu" (I almost did) denotes the nearness of the act. Then he resumed with His saying: ﴿I conceal it so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives﴾, meaning: it will come upon you suddenly, so that every soul may be recompensed for what it has done of good and evil. This is the explanation of Ibn al-Anbari.

The fifth opinion: ﴿akaadu uhfiha﴾ means "I almost reveal it." It has been recited as "ukhfiha" with a fatha on the alif. The meaning of revealing in this reading is more established in the language. The poet said:

(If you bury the disease, we shall not conceal it, and if you declare war, we shall not sit idle.)

The meaning of "lā nukhfihi" (we shall not conceal it) is: we shall not reveal it.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So let not one who does not believe in it avert you from it﴾, meaning: let not those who do not affirm it prevent you from believing in it. ﴿Who does not believe in it﴾, meaning: who does not affirm it as true.

And His saying: ﴿and follows his desire, and so perishes﴾, meaning: and so is ruined.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on surah 20, verse 17:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Musa?﴾ This is a question of confirmation (su'al taqrir), and not a question of inquiry (su'al istifham). Its wisdom lies in fixing and affirming in him that it is a staff, so that when God turns it into a serpent, he knows that it is a great miracle. This is also a statement in the manner of the Arabs: a man says to another, "Do you know this?" while he has no doubt that the other knows it, and he intends by it that the other's acknowledgment with his tongue be joined to his knowledge in his heart.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 18:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "It is my staff; I lean upon it"﴾. That is: I rely upon it.

And His saying: ﴿and I beat down (leaves) with it for my sheep﴾. That is: I strike with it (the leaves of the trees, so that my sheep may graze on them). ʿIkrimah recited: "wa-ahussu bihā ʿalā ghanamī" with an unpointed sīn (wa-ahuss bihā ʿalā ghanamī). The difference between hashsh (hush) and hassh (hass) is that hashsh is the beating of trees and the knocking of leaves from them, while hass is driving the sheep.

His saying: ﴿and I have in it other uses﴾. That is: other needs. Among those needs, the scholars of the meanings (ahl al-maʿānī) said: he would kill snakes with it, fight off beasts of prey with it, carry provisions and supplies with it, tie the rope to it when drawing water from the well, and shade himself with it when he sat. It is related from al-Ḍaḥḥāk that it would give light for him at night like a lamp. Wahb said: the staff was of myrtle from Paradise, its length was twelve cubits, it had two branches, and on it was a hook. It is related from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr that he said: the name of the staff was "whatever he wished" (kāna ism al-ʿaṣā mā shāʾ). And they recited in (the meaning of) hashsh:

("I beat down with the staff upon my sheep... from the tender arak and bashām trees.")

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on surah 20, verse 19:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said, "Throw it down, O Moses."﴾ That is: cast it away.

And His words ﴿So he threw it﴾ mean: he cast it down.

And His words ﴿and behold, it was a snake, moving swiftly﴾ mean: it came and went. Muhammad ibn Ishaq mentioned that Musa (peace be upon him) looked and behold, the staff had become a snake of the greatest size of snakes, its two forks had become two jaws, and its crook had become a mane that quivered like the stallion camel's (al-bitarik). Its eyes blazed like fire, and it passed by a rock like a kneeling camel and swallowed it, and it had fangs that crushed trees. Musa saw a tremendous matter and fled. Then he remembered the command of his Lord, so he stopped, feeling shy.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 21:

The words of the Most High: ﴿Take it and do not fear﴾. When Musa fled, Allah the Most High said to him: ﴿Come forward and do not fear﴾. When he came forward, He said: ﴿Take it﴾.

It is related in the account that Musa was wearing a woolen cloak (mudraʿa), which he had reinforced with sticks. When Allah said to him: ﴿Take it﴾, he wrapped the end of the cloak's sleeve around his hand. So Allah commanded him to uncover his hand, and he uncovered it and placed it in the mouth (shidq) of the serpent. Then it was a staff as it had been, and his hand was in its forked part (shuʿba).

Some of them mentioned that when he wrapped the sleeve of the cloak around his hand, an angel said to him: "Do you see, if Allah permitted what you are wary of, would your cloak avail you?" He said: "I am weak; I was created from weakness."

And His words: ﴿We shall return it to its former state﴾. That is, to its original form. The word is in the accusative because its meaning is "to its original form," and so "ilā" (to) was omitted and the word became accusative.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 22:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And draw your hand close to your side﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions: first, "to your side"; second, "to your upper arm." The jinah (wing) is the upper arm up to the base of the armpit. The poet said:

(I lowered toward them the wing of affection from myself... over a shoulder whose two sides are the people of Ahl and Marhab)

As for His words: ﴿it will come forth white, without any defect﴾, meaning radiant and shining, free from any harm or blemish. Here "su'" (defect) carries the meaning of leprosy (baras).

Qatadah said: the hand had a bright light like the light of the sun and the moon, shining by night and by day.

As for His words: ﴿another sign﴾, meaning another proof.

"And His saying: ﴿That We may show you of Our greatest signs﴾. That is, the great ones. Ibn ʿAbbas said: The greater of the two signs is his hand; when he would bring it out from beneath his armpit, they would see a radiance and a light in it that dazzled the eyes, and when he returned it to his armpit and took it out, it would return to what it had been."

And His words: ﴿Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed﴾. That is: he exceeded the limit in disobedience and rebellion. It is said that his name was al-Walid ibn Mus'ab, and he was the richest of the Pharaohs who were in Egypt.

Almighty God's words: ﴿My Lord, expand my breast for me﴾, meaning: make my breast spacious for the truth. Moses feared Pharaoh greatly, because of his intense might and the abundance of his troops, so his heart became constricted at being sent to Pharaoh out of fear. Therefore he asked God, exalted is He, to widen his heart for the truth, so that he would know that no one can do anything to him except by God's permission, or harm him except by His will.
And His saying: ﴿And ease for me my affair﴾, i.e., make easy for me the matter for which You have sent me.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 27:

His saying: ﴿And untie the knot from my tongue﴾. The people of tafsir (exegesis) said: There was a knot on Musa's tongue from his taking of the ember, and placing it in his mouth. The cause of this was that the wife of Pharaoh brought Musa to Pharaoh and placed him in his lap, and he took hold of Pharaoh's beard. In another narration, he slapped Pharaoh's face with a slap, so Pharaoh became angry and said: "This is my enemy," and wanted to kill him. Pharaoh's wife said: "He is a child, who does not understand or discern, and he does not distinguish between the jewel and the ember." So a tray of embers and a tray of jewels were brought for him, and he took the ember and placed it in his mouth, so his tongue was burned, and a knot remained upon it. Some of them mentioned that he wanted to take the jewel, but Jibril (Gabriel) turned his hand towards the ember.
And His saying: ﴿that they may understand my speech﴾, that is: that they may comprehend my speech.

﴿And appoint for me a minister from my family﴾. The wazir (minister) is one who supports you in a matter, that is, who helps you and bears from you some of its burden; and the wazir of a ruler is one who bears from him some of what is upon him.

And His saying: ﴿Aaron, my brother﴾. Aaron was four years older than him. He was more eloquent in speech, more beautiful in appearance, handsomer, and fairer. Moses was dark-complexioned, with a prominent nose and curly hair.

And His saying ﴿Strengthen my back through him﴾ means: strengthen my back by means of him. It is said: there was never anyone more fortunate toward his brother, nor more beneficial to his brother, than Musa was to Harun.
"And His saying: ﴿and make him a partner in my task﴾, meaning: prophethood and the discharge of the message."
"And His saying: ﴿That we may glorify You much﴾ — i.e., that we may pray to You much."
﴿And glorify You abundantly﴾ — we will cooperate in remembering You.
﴿Indeed You were ever Seeing of us﴾, i.e., Aware, Knowing.
Allah the Exalted's saying: ﴿He said, "You have been given your request, O Moses."﴾ That is, You have been given everything you asked for.
And His saying: ﴿And We had already bestowed favor upon you another time﴾, meaning: We bestowed favor upon you another time besides this time.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿When We inspired your mother with what is inspired﴾. He mentioned His favours upon him and enumerated them to him, so that he would recognise them and increase in thanking Him.

And His words: ﴿When We inspired your mother with what is inspired﴾, meaning: We caused your mother to receive inspiration (ilham) of what is inspired, that is, of what is inspired (ilham) to be received.

And His saying, ﴿that cast him﴾, meaning: We inspired her that she should cast him.

His saying, ﴿into the chest﴾: it is a thing made of wood.

And His saying, ﴿cast him into the sea (al-yamm)﴾: al-yamm is the sea. It is also said that al-yamm here is the Nile, and the Arabs call abundant water "sea" (bahr).

It is narrated that when the Muslims reached the Tigris (Dijlah) on the day they conquered al-Mada'in, they said, "How shall we act, when this sea lies between us and them?" Then they plunged into the Tigris with their horses and crossed, and the account goes on to its end.

And His saying, ﴿and let the sea cast him onto the shore﴾: in the story, the water threw him to the landing-place of Pharaoh's palace. It is also narrated that she cast him into the Nile, the Nile cast him into the sea, and then the sea cast him onto the shore.

And His saying, ﴿and I cast upon you love from Me﴾: Ikrimah said, "No one saw him without loving him." Qatadah said, "There was a comeliness in his eyes that captivated (hearts)."

And His saying, ﴿and that you might be brought up under My eye﴾: meaning, you would be reared and nourished under My watch. This is like His saying, ﴿When your sister walked and said, "Shall I direct you to one who will take charge of him?" So We returned you to your mother that her eye might be comforted and she would not grieve. And you killed a soul, but We saved you from distress and tested you with a severe testing﴾, the Exalted: ﴿and make the ark under Our eyes﴾. If it is said: there is no one in the world who is not reared and nourished under the sight and watch of God, so what is the meaning of singling out Moses? The answer: God, exalted is He, showed in the gentle care of Moses' upbringing what He did not show in the upbringing of anyone else, so the specification points to that gentle care.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 40:

And His saying: ﴿When your sister walked along﴾ — we will mention this in Surat al-Qasas, God willing, Most High.

And His saying: ﴿Shall I direct you to someone who will take charge of him?﴾ — meaning: to a woman who will nurse him and take him to herself.

And His saying: ﴿So We returned you to your mother﴾ — that is: We sent you back.

And His saying: ﴿So that her eye may be cooled﴾ — we have already explained the meaning of "coolness of the eye," and it is an indication of her joy and delight at his existence.

And His saying: ﴿and she would not grieve﴾ — that is: grief would depart from her.

And His saying: ﴿and you killed a soul﴾ — that is, the Copt; we will mention it later, God willing, Most High.

And His saying: ﴿So We delivered you from distress﴾ — that is: from killing. It was also said: from the distress of the chest (ark) and the distress of the sea.

And His saying: ﴿and We tested you with a testing﴾ — that is: We tried you time after time. It was also said: a trial after a trial. And it is said: We purified you with a purification.

Among the well-known reports: Sa'id ibn Jubayr asked Abdullah ibn 'Abbas about His saying: ﴿and We tested you with a testing﴾. He said: "You go out (in the morning) on one morning." When he came the next day, he (Ibn 'Abbas) began with the story of Musa from its beginning, and started enumerating to him, one by one, things from his birth in the year the sons were killed, and his being cast into the water, and his being placed in the chest, and his falling into the hand of Pharaoh, and Pharaoh's slapping of his face, and his taking the live coal, then his killing of the Copt, then his flight to Madyan... to the end of the story as it is related. And every time he mentioned one of these things, he would say: "That is (from) the trials, O son of Jubayr," until he had counted all of them.

And His saying: ﴿Then you stayed for years among the people of Madyan﴾ — meaning: you tended the sheep.

And His saying: ﴿Then you came according to a measure, O Musa﴾ — that is: according to the measure of prophethood and messengership. Ibn 'Abbas said: God did not send any prophet except at the age of forty, and Musa came to his Lord when he was forty years old, so God gave him prophecy and sent him. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿Then you came according to a measure, O Musa﴾. It was also said its meaning is: you came at an appointed time, O Musa, and this appointment was not with Musa; rather it was an appointment in God's decree, Most High. And it is said: you arrived at the time that was decreed, that is, you met at it. The poet said:

(He attained the caliphate when it was decreed for him, / like Musa who arrived at a measure.)

And His words: ﴿And I have chosen you for Myself﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is, "I have chosen you for My affair, and made you the one who stands with My proof and the one who speaks between Me and My creation, as if I am the One who established the proof against them and addressed them." Some of them said: its meaning is, "I have made you responsible for handling the fulfilment of a matter from among My own specific affairs." The ṣanī'a (protégé, one raised and trained) of a person is his close intimate and the one he has trained when he prepares him for an important matter of his affairs.

Your Lord says: "Go, you and your brother, with My signs" (Qur'an 20:42). That is, with My proofs.

And His words: "and do not slacken in My remembrance" (Qur'an 20:42). That is, do not weaken in My remembrance. Ibn Mas'ud recited it as: "and do not weaken in My remembrance."
"And His saying: ﴿Go, both of you, to Pharaoh; indeed, he has transgressed.﴾ — we have already explained it."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 44:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Speak to him with gentle speech﴾. Its meaning: deal with him gently (dārīhi, from mudārāh, "gentle dealing") and be kind to him. It is also said its meaning is: address him by his kunya (teknonym). The scholars differed regarding his kunya. Some of them said: his kunya is Abu al-Walid; others said: Abu Murra; and others said: Abu al-'Abbas. And God knows best.

And His saying: ﴿Perhaps he will be mindful or fear﴾. That is: he will take heed and be afraid. If it is said: the word ﴿perhaps﴾ (la'alla) expresses hope, so how can He make them hopeful regarding his submission, when it has already been decreed that he will not submit? We say: its meaning is: go with your hope and expectation, while God's decree stands beyond your command. Some of them said: he did become mindful and feared, but only at a time when neither the reminder nor the fear benefited him. We have explained this in Surah Yunus.

Regarding His saying: ﴿Speak to him with gentle speech﴾, there are well-known sayings. Some of them said: this is your gentleness toward one who says, "I am the god," so how is your gentleness toward one who says, "You are the God"? This is your gentleness toward the disbelievers, so how is your gentleness toward the righteous? This is your gentleness toward one who denied You, so how is your gentleness toward one who affirmed You as One? This is your affection toward one whom you oppose, so how is it toward one whom you befriend and call upon?

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 45:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "Our Lord, we fear that he will hasten against us or that he will transgress."﴾ He means: that he will rush and hasten to punish us before we show him the signs.

It is related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he said: Musa used to fear Pharaoh with a great fear, and whenever he entered upon him he would say, "O Allah, I seek refuge in You from his evil, and I place You against his throat." So Allah, exalted is He, transferred that fear to Pharaoh, and whenever he saw Musa, he would urinate on his garments as a donkey urinates.

In some of the musnads, on the narration of Ibn Mas'ud, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "If one of you enters upon a ruler whose arrogance he fears, let him say: O Allah, I seek refuge in You from his evil and the evil of his factions, lest any of them hasten against me or transgress. Mighty is Your protection, glorified is Your praise, and there is no god but You."

Almighty Allah's words: ﴿He said: "Do not fear; indeed I am with you both, hearing and seeing"﴾. That is: I hear your supplication and will answer it, and I see your affair with Pharaoh and will repel him from you.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 47:

The Exalted's saying: ﴿So go to him and say, "Indeed, we are messengers of your Lord, so send with us the Children of Israel"﴾. That is, release them and set them free from your labours. We have already explained that he (Pharaoh) used to assign them arduous tasks, and he had imposed taxes upon them.

His saying: ﴿And do not torment them﴾ — we have already explained this.

His saying: ﴿We have certainly come to you with a sign from your Lord﴾ — a clear proof from your Lord.

His saying: ﴿And peace be upon those who follow guidance﴾. The intended meaning is not a greeting to Pharaoh. Rather, the intended meaning is that whoever follows guidance has been safe from the punishment of Allah. Some have said: its meaning is, "Whoever submits (aslama) will be safe (salima)."

It is related in some reports from al-Suddi that Musa, peace be upon him, said to Pharaoh: "Believe in Allah, and you will have a youth in which you never grow old, a kingdom that will not be taken from you, and pleasure in food, drink and marriage until you die; then, when you die, you will enter Paradise." This statement pleased him, and he did not decide any matter without Haman. He said: "Let me consider this." When Haman entered upon him, he said to him: "Did you not see that this man who came to us said such-and-such?" Previously he had called him "the sorcerer," but on that day he did not call him the sorcerer. Haman said to him: "I thought you had an opinion and intellect! Do you wish to become one who is nurtured after you were a lord, and a servant after you were one who is worshipped?" So he overcame him in his opinion, and he refused Musa what he wanted from him.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, it has been revealed to us that the punishment will be upon whoever denies and turns away.﴾ That is: denies the signs of Allah, and turns away from obedience to Allah.
"Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He said, 'Who then is your Lord, O Moses?'﴾ The meaning is apparent."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 50:

And His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Our Lord is He who gave everything its creation, then guided it.﴾ Al-Hasan said: He gave everything what would suit it, then guided it to it. Mujahid said: its meaning is that He gave everything a form, then guided it to its benefits, from food, drink and marriage.

There is a third opinion in this: that He gave every animal its mate, then guided it to its coupling, and that every male is guided to how it approaches the female. It was narrated from Abu Sabit that he said: The animals were left unexplained, except for four: they know their Creator, they seek their provision, they defend themselves, and they know how to approach their females.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on surah 20, verse 51:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Pharaoh said, "What then is the state of the former generations?"﴾ Its meaning is: what is the state of the former generations? He meant by it: what is their condition regarding what you have called me to?

It is also said: when Moses called him to acknowledge the Resurrection (al-ba'th), he asked and said: what is the state of the former generations regarding the Resurrection? And it is said that he turned to this speech out of obstinacy (ta'annut) and evasion of the answer (i'tidal 'an al-jawab).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 52:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿He said: Its knowledge is with my Lord﴾, meaning: the knowledge of the earlier generations is with my Lord.

[The words ﴿in a Book﴾: al-Kalbi said: it is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz).]

And His words ﴿My Lord neither errs nor forgets﴾, meaning: my Lord does not make a mistake. Tha'lab said: nothing about its place escapes Him. It was also said: it is not hidden from my Lord. Al-Hasan recited ﴿lā yuḍillu rabbī﴾ with a damma on the yā' (yuḍillu), from al-idlal (causing to go astray), and it is said: ﴿lā yuḍillu rabbī﴾ means my Lord is not heedless of it.

And His words ﴿nor does He forget﴾, meaning: He does not leave it, so that He punishes the disbeliever and rewards the believer. It is also said: it is forgetting in its literal sense. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami recited ﴿wa-lā yansā﴾ in the passive form (of the verb whose subject is not named).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 53:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Who made the earth for you a cradle﴾, and it is read "mahdan" (a cradle). Up to this point is the speech of Pharaoh with Musa and his reply to him. His saying: ﴿Who made the earth for you a cradle﴾ is the beginning of speech from God, and its meaning: a resting place (mustaqarran).

His saying: ﴿and threaded for you therein roads﴾, that is: He made easy and smooth for you therein paths.

His saying: ﴿and sent down from the sky water﴾, that is: the rain.

His saying: ﴿then We brought forth thereby pairs﴾, that is: kinds: the red, the yellow, and the green.

His saying: ﴿of diverse plants﴾, that is: of scattered plants.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 54:

And His saying: ﴿Eat and graze your livestock﴾, meaning: eat, and send your livestock out to graze.

And His saying: ﴿Indeed in that are signs for those of intellect (ulī al-nuhā)﴾. Tha'lab said: "For those of reason (ulī al-ʿuqūl)." It was also said: "For those whose opinion is decisive (alladhīna yantahī ilā raʾyihim)." And it was said: "For those who restrain themselves from acts of disobedience and hold back from them by their reason."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 55:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿From it We created you﴾, i.e., from the earth.

And His saying: ﴿And into it We will return you﴾, i.e., at the time of death.

And His saying: ﴿And from it We will bring you forth once again﴾, i.e., at the time of the gathering (al-hashr). If it is said: at the beginning, we were not brought out of the earth, so how does He say "once again" (tara ukhra)? We say: its meaning is, "And from it We will create you once again," and the meaning is sound on this reading.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 56:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We showed him all of Our signs﴾. These are the nine signs that were given to Musa, peace be upon him.

And His saying: ﴿But he denied and refused﴾. That is: he denied the Oneness (tawhid), and refused to accept faith (iman).

Almighty God's words: ﴿He said: "Have you come to us to drive us out of our land with your magic, O Moses?"﴾ Its meaning: that you may seize our land, so that sovereignty and authority will be yours, and you may expel whomever you wish and admit whomever you wish.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 58:

His words: ﴿Then we will surely bring you a magic like it.﴾ He means: like your magic.

And His words: ﴿So set up between us and you an appointment﴾, meaning: an appointment for gathering.

And His words: ﴿which neither we nor you will fail to keep.﴾ Meaning: neither we nor you will fail to keep it.

And His words: ﴿a place equitable (suwa)﴾. It has been read with a nominative vowel (sawan, sūwan-type reading with raf') and it has been read with a kasra. Its meaning is: a just place. It was said: an impartial place. And it is said: in a level place where nothing of what one of us does to the other is hidden from anyone there.

Ibn Faris said: This is the view of al-Hasan. It is also said: "makanan sawa" means a place that is equidistant in terms of distance to it.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 59:

The words of the Most High: ﴿Your appointment is the Day of Adornment (al-Zinah)﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: "The Day of Adornment is a festival day for them; they used to gather for it." And it is said: it is the Day of Fayruz (al-Fayruz, the Persian New Year festival). It is related from 'Ata': that he disliked adorning oneself for festivals, and he said: "It is among the practices of the disbelievers."

And His words: ﴿and that the people be gathered at mid-morning (duha)﴾, meaning: at the beginning of the day. It has been the custom that festivals take place at the start of the day, and likewise the gathering of people for affairs is most often at the start of the day.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 60:

The words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿Then Pharaoh turned away﴾, mean: he turned away (fa-a'rada). It was also said: Pharaoh took charge of the matter (wallā al-amr Fir'awn).

His words, ﴿then gathered his scheming﴾, mean: his deceit (makr) and his stratagem (ḥīla).

His words, ﴿then came back﴾, mean: then he came with the appointed meeting (bi-l-maw'id).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 61:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Musa said to them, "Woe to you! Do not fabricate against Allah a lie, lest He destroy you with a punishment. And he has failed who fabricates."﴾ Al-Dahhak reported from Ibn 'Abbas: Pharaoh gathered seventy thousand sorcerers. Muqatil mentioned fifteen thousand. Some mentioned "a little over seventy men," and this is the well-known view.

His saying: ﴿Woe to you! Do not fabricate against Allah a lie﴾ means: do not invent lies against Allah; its meaning is: do not lie about Allah.

His saying: ﴿then He will destroy you with a punishment﴾ — the yā' is with a fatha (فيسحتكم, read yusihtakum with the verb in the nasb form). It has also been recited with a ḍamma on the yā' (فيسحتكم, read yusihtukum), and its meaning is uprooting (al-isti'sal), i.e., He will uproot you with the punishment. Al-Farazdaq said in verse:

(And the bite of a time, O son of Marwan, has left nothing of the wealth except what is uprooted or what is stripped bare.)

Some distinguished between the rafʿ (ḍamma) and the fatḥa, saying: with the naṣb (fatḥa), it means that nothing remains; with the rafʿ (ḍamma), it means that some remnant remains. The more correct view is that there is no difference. It was also said: "fa-yasḥitakum" means "shahida lakum" (testified for you)... 

His saying: ﴿And he has failed who fabricates﴾ means: he who fabricates has lost and perished.

Almighty Allah's words: ﴿So they disputed among themselves about their affair and secretly conferred﴾. Qatadah said: This refers to the magicians, and their secret conferring was that they said: "If what Moses brings is magic, we will overcome him. And if he overcomes us, then it is a matter of his own [power]." It is also narrated that they said: "If he overcomes us, we will follow him."

The words of the Most High: ﴿They said, "Indeed, these two are certainly sorcerers"﴾. Know that this verse is difficult in terms of Arabic grammar, and it has three readings (qira'at).

Abu 'Amr recited: "Inna hadhayni la-sahiran" (إن هذين لساحران). Hafs recited: "Inna hadhani la-sahiran" (إن هذان لساحران). The rest recited: "Inna hadhani la-sahiran" (إن هذان لساحران).

As for the reading of Abu 'Amr, it is the one that is correct according to the apparent rules of Arabic. Abu 'Amr claimed that "hadhani" (هذان) is a scribal error in the mushaf (the written codex of the Qur'an).

It is related from 'Uthman, may God be pleased with him, that he said: "I see a lahn (grammatical error) in the mushaf; the Arabs will straighten it with their tongues." A similar report is related from 'Aisha, may God be pleased with her.

As for the reading of Hafs, it is also correct in Arabic, because when "inna" is light (mukhaffafah), what follows it is in the nominative case, and its meaning is: "These two are none but sorcerers."

As for the reading of the majority, which is the most sound, al-Zajjaj said: "We do not accept the reading of Abu 'Amr in this verse, because it contradicts the mushaf." As for the explanation of His saying ﴿Inna hadhani﴾, it has several aspects in Arabic. The early grammarians said: "It is in the sense of innahu hadhani (إنه هذان), so the pronoun (ha') is omitted, and there are many such examples in Arabic." The second aspect: this form (hadhani) is the dialect of Kinanah and Khath'am (and Zubayd), and al-Kisa'i said: it is the dialect of Bani al-Harith ibn Ka'b from Kinanah. Al-Kisa'i recited a line of poetry:

(Take from me, between his ears, a blow that the barren earth calls him to)

Another recited:

(Indeed her father and her father's father have reached the furthest point in glory)

And they also recited:

(Which she-camel, a rider sees her; they flew above them, a flying above them)

Meaning: "above them" (ʿalayhinna).

Al-Kisa'i said: according to this dialect they say: "The two Zayds came to me (atani al-zaydan), I saw the two Zayds, and I passed by the two Zayds," and they never drop the dual alif in any of these.

As for the third aspect, which is the most correct of the aspects, since the Qur'an should not be interpreted according to a remote dialect, it is that the meaning of His saying ﴿Inna hadhani﴾ is "Yes, these two," as the poet said:

(The blame-makers of the morning have reproached me, and I reproach them)

(And they say, "Gray hair has overtaken you, and you have grown old," so I said, "Indeed," meaning "Yes.")

It is narrated that a Bedouin came to 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr seeking something, but his desire was not fulfilled. The Bedouin said: "May God curse the she-camel that carried me to you." Ibn al-Zubayr said: "Inna, and its owner," meaning: "Yes, and its owner."

In the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "Inna dhaka illa sahiran" (إن ذاك إلا ساحران), and this is a shadhdh (irregular) reading.

As for His saying ﴿They want to drive you out of your land by their magic﴾, we have already explained it.

As for His saying ﴿and to do away with your most excellent way of life﴾, meaning: with the upright way that you are upon, for they used to think that they were upon a straight religion. "Al-muthla" is the feminine of "al-amthal" (the best). As for Ibn 'Abbas, he said: "Your most excellent way (bi-tariqatikum al-muthla)" means: the noble men.

Qatadah said: He meant by it the Children of Israel, and they were people of wealth and honor.

So they said: "They want to take these people away." The Arabs say: "These are the way (tariqat) of the people," meaning: their nobles.

Some of them said: its meaning is "the people of your most excellent way."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 64:

And His saying: ﴿So gather your plot⁠﴾. It is also read with a wasl (connected alif): "fa-jami'u" (then gather). As for His saying ﴿fa-ajma'u﴾ with qat' (the hamzah of cutting, i.e., ajma'a), its meaning is resolve and determination. Al-Azhari said: its implied sense is: "Resolve, all of you, upon his plot, being united in it, and do not disagree, lest your affair be undermined." As for His saying "fa-jami'u" with wasl, its meaning is: bring every plot you have, so that you may oppose Musa.

And His saying: ﴿Then come in ranks⁠﴾. Abu 'Ubaydah said: "lined up" (muṣṭaffīn). Others said: the ṣaff is the place of prayer (al-muṣallā), and its meaning is: then come to the appointed place.

And His saying: ﴿And he has certainly succeeded today who prevails⁠﴾, i.e., whoever has the upper hand today has prospered and won.
"Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They said, "O Musa, either you throw or we will be the first to throw."﴾ Its meaning: choose, either you throw first, or we throw first."

"The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿He said, "Rather, you throw first."﴾ That is, begin by casting, you yourselves. If someone says: their casting was disbelief and sorcery, so is it permissible that Musa would command them to cast what is sorcery and disbelief? The answer to this is from two aspects. The first: this is a command in the sense of a statement (amr bi-ma'na al-khabar), and its meaning is: if your casting is a proof in your view, then cast. The second: he commanded them to cast with the intention of nullifying their sorcery by what would be cast from his staff, and this is permissible.

And His words: ﴿Then their ropes and staffs, by their sorcery, appeared to him as though they were moving.﴾ It is also read with the yā' and the tā' as "yukhayyalu" (it appears). Whoever reads with the tā', it refers back to the staffs and ropes, and the verb is feminine because it is a plural (of things). As for the yā', it refers to the casting. In the narration: when they cast the ropes and staffs, Musa and the people saw as if the earth was filled with serpents, and they were "yas'a," meaning moving about and coming back. Know that takhayyul is what has no basis in reality. It is said: they took hold of people's eyes, so they thought and supposed that they were serpents. It is also said: their ropes and staffs took a course to this side and a course to that side.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on surah 20, verse 67:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So Moses sensed fear within himself﴾. That is: he found fear in his soul. The scholars differed concerning this fear, according to two views. The first: that it was the fear of human nature. The second: that he feared for the people, lest the matter become confused for them, so that they would not believe. And it is said: he feared for his people that they might doubt and turn back from faith.
Allah's words: ﴿Do not fear; indeed, you are the superior one.﴾ That is, victory and triumph are yours.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 69:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And throw what is in your right hand; it will swallow up what they have made﴾. That is: it will seize (talqaf) and gulp down (tablaʿ).

In the narrative: it opened its mouth and swallowed everything of the staffs and ropes that passed by it, while Pharaoh was laughing and thinking it was magic. Then it made for Pharaoh's dome, and its height in the air was [forty] cubits, and it opened its mouth to the extent of eighty cubits, and wanted to swallow the dome. Pharaoh called out: "O Musa, by the right of the upbringing (I gave you)!" He said: So he came and took it, and it returned to being a staff as it had been.

And His saying: ﴿Indeed, what they have made is only the plot of a magician﴾. It was recited as "sāḥir" and it was recited as "siḥr." So His saying ﴿the plot of a magician﴾ means: the trick of a magician.

And His saying: ﴿the plot of magic﴾ means: the trick of one who practises magic.

And His saying: ﴿and the magician does not prosper wherever he comes﴾. In the exegesis, its meaning is: wherever he is found, he is killed.

And in some of the musnads, on the authority of Jundub ibn ʿAbd Allah, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "If you seize a magician, then kill him," and he recited His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and the magician does not prosper wherever he comes﴾.

The Exalted's saying: ﴿So the sorcerers were thrown down prostrate﴾. We have already explained this before.

And His saying: ﴿They said, "We have believed in the Lord of Harun and Musa."﴾ That is: in the God of Harun and Musa. He placed Harun before Musa in accordance with the rhythm of the verse endings (ru'us al-ayat).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 71:

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Pharaoh said: "Have you believed in him before I give you permission?"﴾ The meaning is apparent.

And His words: ﴿Indeed, he is your chief (kabir) who taught you magic.﴾ That is: your teacher (mu'allimukum) who taught you magic. al-Kisa'i related that the Arabs say: "I returned from the presence of my kabir," meaning my teacher.

And His words: ﴿Then I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides.﴾ The meaning is apparent.

And His words: ﴿And I will surely crucify you upon the trunks of palm trees.﴾ Its meaning is: "upon the trunks of palm trees." The word fi ("in") is mentioned because the one crucified is stretched lengthwise along the trunk, so the trunk encloses him.

And His words: ﴿And you will surely know which of us is more severe in punishment and more lasting.﴾ That is: is it I who am stronger, or the Lord of Musa? al-Kalbi mentioned that Pharaoh did cut off their hands and feet and crucified them. Others mentioned that he was not able to do so against them, and they cited His words, exalted is He: ﴿They shall not reach you with Our signs; you and whoever follows you will be the victors.﴾

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 72:

The words of the Most High: ﴿They said: "We will not prefer you over what has come to us of the clear proofs"﴾, meaning: we will not choose you. ﴿over what has come to us of the clear proofs﴾, meaning: the evidences. Their argument was that they said: "If this is magic, then where are our ropes and our staffs?" It was also said: "of the clear proofs" means: the certainty and the knowledge.

As for His words: ﴿and Him who originated us﴾, there are two opinions regarding it. The first: (His words) "and we will not prefer you over Him who originated us." The second: that it is an oath.

As for His words: ﴿So decree what you will decree﴾, meaning: do what you will do.

As for His words: ﴿You can only decree concerning this worldly life﴾, meaning: your command and your authority are only in this worldly life, and it will soon pass away.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 73:

And His saying: ﴿Indeed, we have believed in our Lord, that He may forgive us our sins﴾. That is: our sins.

And His saying: ﴿and what you compelled us to do of magic﴾. If it is said: How can this be right, since they came of their own choice, and swore by the might of Pharaoh that they would have the victory, as mentioned in another passage? The answer to this is that it has been narrated from al-Hasan al-Basri that he said: Pharaoh used to force a group of people to learn magic, so that his own (knowledge of it) would not vanish. He had compelled them at the beginning to learn it, so they meant this.

And His saying: ﴿And Allah is better and more enduring﴾. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said its meaning is: Allah is better in reward if He is obeyed, and more enduring in punishment if He is disobeyed. It is said: the command of the ruler is a compulsion; therefore they said: "and what you compelled us to do of magic." When they prostrated, Allah Most High showed them their places in Paradise and what He had prepared for them of reward and honour, so when they raised their heads, having [seen] this, they said what they said.

And from ʿIkrimah: "They awoke as sorcerers, and they went to evening as martyrs."

It is also narrated that when al-Hasan reached this verse he would say: How strange are a people, disbelieving sorcerers, among the most intensely disbelieving of people, in whose hearts faith became firmly established when they said what they said, and they did not care about the punishment of Pharaoh. And you see one of these men keeping faith for sixty years, then selling it for a small price.

In the narrative: Pharaoh's wife used to inquire on that day as to who would have the victory. When she was informed that the victory had gone to Moses, she openly displayed her faith in Allah. This was reported to Pharaoh, so he sent a group and said: "Look at the largest rock; if she persists in her statement, then cast the rock upon her." Allah Most High showed her her place in Paradise, and took her soul. So they came and cast the rock onto a dead body.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 74:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal (mujriman)﴾. Some of them said: this is from the speech of the magicians. Others said: it is the beginning of speech from Allah the Exalted. His words: ﴿mujriman﴾, i.e., a polytheist (mushrikan).

And His words: ﴿Indeed, for him is the Fire of Hell; he will neither die therein nor live﴾, i.e., he will not live a life from which he benefits, nor will he die and find rest. It is said: their souls will remain suspended at their throats, neither leaving them so that they die, nor settling in their places so that they live. The poet said:

(Is there anyone for a soul that dies, so that its misery ends, and does not live a life that has any sweetness to it?)

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 75:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever comes to Him as a believer, having done righteous deeds﴾, meaning: who has performed the obligations (al-fara'id). Al-Hasan said: whoever performs the obligations has completed the faith, and whoever does not perform the obligations has not completed the faith.

And His saying: ﴿Then those will have the high ranks﴾ — al-'ulā is the plural of al-'ulyā, and al-'ulyā is the feminine of al-A'lā.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 76:

His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿Gardens of Eden﴾. We have explained this before. In some of the exegetical works, it is reported from ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "The Garden of Eden is a palace that has ten thousand doors, and none knows its vastness except Allah." It is also said: "There is a river in Paradise, and on its two banks are the palaces of the Gardens."

And His statement: ﴿Beneath which rivers flow﴾. We have explained this.

And His statement: ﴿Abiding therein﴾, meaning: remaining therein.

And His statement: ﴿That is the recompense of one who purifies himself﴾, meaning: the purification from sins. It is also said: it is the recompense of one who says, "There is no god but Allah."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 77:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We revealed to Moses, "Travel by night with My servants"﴾. That is: travel with them by night.

And His saying: ﴿So strike for them a dry path through the sea﴾. That is: having dryness (yabs), and it was said: dry (yabisan), meaning there is no moisture in it and no dampness.

And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do not fear being overtaken, nor be apprehensive﴾. It is narrated that when they reached the sea they said: "O Moses, the sea is before us, and Pharaoh and his army are behind us." So Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Do not fear being overtaken, nor be apprehensive﴾. That is: do not fear that Pharaoh will overtake you from behind, nor be apprehensive that the sea will drown you in front of you. Hamzah recited "wa-la takhaf" in the imperative mood.

The commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 78:

Allah's statement: ﴿Then Pharaoh followed them with his hosts﴾. It is recited as "fa-atbaʿahum" (فأتبعهم), and it is recited as "fa-ttabaʿahum" (فاتبعهم). As for His statement ﴿fa-atbaʿahum﴾, it means: he sent his hosts after them (بعث في إثرهم جنوده).

And His statement ﴿fa-ttabaʿahum﴾ means: he followed them with his army (اتبعهم بجنده).

And His statement ﴿Then the sea covered them with that which covered them﴾: its meaning is that the sea covered them, namely the water that drowned them. It is said: "the sea covered them with what covered the people of Moses," so the people of Moses were saved and they were drowned. It is also said: "the sea covered them with what destroyed them."

And His saying: ﴿And Pharaoh led his people astray, and did not guide [them]﴾ — i.e., he did not give them guidance (irshad). This is a response to Pharaoh's saying: ﴿And I show you only the way of right guidance﴾.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 80:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O Children of Israel, We delivered you from your enemy﴾, that is, from your enemies. It is also said: He meant by it Pharaoh alone.

And His saying: ﴿And We made appointment with you at the right side of the Mount﴾. In the exegesis, it is that God, Exalted is He, promised Moses that He would give him a Book from Himself, which is the Torah. This is the meaning of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We made appointment with you at the right side of the Mount﴾, that is, for the giving of the Book.

And His saying: ﴿And We sent down upon you the manna and the quail﴾. We have explained it in Surat al-Baqarah.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 81:

And His saying: ﴿Eat of the good things with which We have provided you﴾, that is: of the lawful (ḥalāl) things with which We have provided you.

And His saying: ﴿and do not transgress therein﴾. That is: do not be ungrateful for the blessing. It is also said: do not mix the unlawful (ḥarām) with the lawful (ḥalāl). And it is related from Ibn ʿAbbās: "Do not store [food], for then it will rot. And had they not stored it, food would never have rotted."

And His saying: ﴿so that My wrath descends upon you﴾. It is recited with kasra and with ḍamma. With kasra (fa-yaḥilla) it means "it becomes due" (yajibu), and with ḍamma (fa-yanzil) it means "it descends" (yanzil).

And His saying: ﴿And whoever has My wrath descend upon him﴾, that is: it descends upon him. It is also recited "wa-man yaḥlul," meaning: it becomes due (yajibu).

And His saying: ﴿then he has indeed fallen﴾, that is: he has perished. And it is related from Shafiyy ibn Māti' al-Aṣbaḥī, who said: "Hawā is a valley in Hell, into which one falls for forty autumns." The meaning of the verse, that is: he has fallen into it.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 82:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And indeed, I am Forgiving toward one who repents﴾, meaning: from polytheism (shirk). ﴿And believes﴾, meaning: believes in Allah.

And His words: ﴿and does righteous deeds﴾, meaning: he performs the obligatory duties (al-fara'id).

And His words: ﴿then remains guided﴾. Regarding this there are several opinions. Ibn 'Abbas said: he did not doubt his faith. From Qatadah, he said: he died upon faith. From Sa'id ibn Jubayr: he adhered to the Sunnah and the Jama'ah. Some of them said: he was sincere (akhlasa). Some of them said: he acted by his deed. From Thabit al-Bunani, he said: he took the Ahl al-Bayt as allies (tawalla Ahl al-Bayt).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 83:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And what has hastened you from your people, O Moses?﴾ In the story: when he came with the seventy at the appointed time, he hastened ahead by himself and left the seventy behind him. So God, exalted is He, said to him: ﴿And what has hastened you from your people, O Moses?﴾ That is, what compelled you to haste?

And His saying: ﴿They are following on my track﴾ — that is, they are coming after me.

And His saying: ﴿And I hastened to You, my Lord, that You might be pleased﴾ — that is, that You might increase in good pleasure. And it is related from some of the early generation (al-salaf) that he hastened out of longing.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 85:

The words of the Most High: ﴿He said, "Indeed, We have tested your people after you,"﴾ meaning: We caused them to fall into fitnah (trial and tribulation).

His words: ﴿and al-Samiri has misled them﴾ meaning: they went astray because of him. We have already explained a portion of this story in Surat al-A'raf. It is related from Wahb, with his chain of narration, from Rashid ibn Sa'd that when God, exalted is He, said this statement to him, [Musa] said: "O Lord, who fashioned the calf?" He said: "al-Samiri." He said: "Who then brought it to life and made the lowing come out of it?" He said: "I did." He said: "Then You misled them, O Lord." So God, exalted is He, said to him: "O (head) of the prophets, I saw that in their hearts, so I made it easy for them."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 86:

And His saying: ﴿So Musa returned to his people, angry and grieved.﴾ That is: greatly saddened by what had befallen his people of trial (fitnah).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He said, "O my people, did your Lord not promise you a good promise?"﴾ Its meaning: what He promised of the sending down of the Book, and of deliverance from Pharaoh and his people, and other things He promised and fulfilled.

And His saying: ﴿Has the time seemed long to you?﴾ Musa had promised that he would return after forty days. When twenty days had passed, they counted the day as twenty and the night as twenty, and said, "The promised time has passed."

And His saying: ﴿Or did you wish that wrath from your Lord should descend upon you?﴾ That is: did you wish to do an act that would make wrath from your Lord obligatory upon you?

And His saying: ﴿So you broke your promise to me﴾ — or "my promise."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 87:

The words of God Most High: ﴿They said, "We did not break our promise to you of our own power.﴾

It has been recited as "bi-mulkina" and also as "bi-mulkina" [with the kasra on the mim]: so His saying "bi-milkina" means by our capacity, and His saying "bi-mulkina" means by our authority. Likewise "bi-malkina" with a fatha on the mim. The best thing said about this is that when a person falls into trial and temptation, he does not possess himself. It is also established from the Prophet (ﷺ) in one of his supplications: "O Allah, if You intend a trial for a people, then take me to You without being tried."

And His saying: ﴿but we were made to carry (ḥummilnā)﴾, and it has been recited as "ḥummilnā." In the account: they borrowed the jewelry of the women of the Copts, then did not return it until they went out to the side of the sea. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿we were made to carry burdens of the ornaments of the people﴾, that is, of the people's jewelry. The word awzār (burdens) means loads, and the jewelry was called awzār because they had taken it by way of loan (ʿāriyya) and did not return it, so it became by way of betrayal.

It is also said: when God Most High drowned them, the sea cast up their jewelry, and he took it, and the spoils were not lawful for them in that time. He named it awzār for this meaning. And the poet said about awzār:

(And I prepared for war its burdens: long spears and male horses.)

And His saying Most High: ﴿so we threw it﴾. It is related that Aaron, peace be upon him, was commanded to dig a pit, then he ordered them to throw that jewelry into it, and he set fire over it. In another account, al-Sāmirī ordered them to do that, and this is the meaning of His saying: ﴿so we threw it﴾.

And His saying: ﴿Thus did al-Sāmirī cast﴾, meaning: al-Sāmirī also cast what he had of the jewelry.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 88:

As for His saying: ﴿So He brought forth for them a calf, a body that had a lowing sound﴾, in the narration: when the fire had purified the gold and silver, al-Samiri came and threw into it a handful of dust, which he had taken from under the hoof of Jibril's horse (peace be upon him), and said: "Be a calf with a lowing sound." So it became a calf that lowed.

As for His saying: ﴿a body﴾, it has been said: a body without a head. It has also been said: a body that neither harms nor benefits. Al-Khalil said: the Arabs call everything that neither eats nor drinks a "body" (jasad), and the calf neither ate nor drank, but it made a sound. The first view is the weakest of the views. They differed regarding the lowing (khuwar). The majority hold that it is the sound of a living calf, and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah and a group. Mujahid said: it is the sound of the rustling of the wind, which would enter its belly and come out, and this is a weak view.

As for His saying: ﴿So they said, "This is your god and the god of Musa, but he has forgotten"﴾, there are two views concerning it. The first: that "This is your god and the god of Musa" means that Musa left it here and went off seeking Him.

The second: its meaning is: "But al-Samiri forgot faith in Allah," i.e., he abandoned it. It has also been said: "But Musa forgot to tell you that this is the God."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 89:

And His saying: ﴿Do they not see that it does not return to them any word?﴾ In some exegeses: the calf lowed (kharra kharāran) one time only and did not repeat it, and this is the meaning of His saying: ﴿that it does not return to them any word﴾. Some of them said: it does not answer them when they call upon it.

And His saying: ﴿and it has no power to harm them or benefit them﴾ — its meaning is apparent.

If it is said: al-Samiri was a disbeliever, and what appeared at his hand was a miracle (mu'jiza); how is it permissible for a miracle to appear at the hand of a disbeliever? The answer: that was a trial (fitna) for the Children of Israel and a test (ibtila') for them.

According to the people of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah), this is permissible, and we do not say that it is a miracle, but rather it is a trial (mihna) and a temptation (fitna).

In some reports: Harun passed by al-Samiri while he was fashioning the calf, and said to him: "What is this?" He said: "It is [something] that benefits and does not harm, so pray for me." Harun said: "O Allah, give him what is in his heart." Then he threw dust into the mouth of the calf and said: "Be a calf that lows," and it was so, by the supplication of Harun.

And the people of knowledge have said: there is no golden calf that lows except through a confusion that falls upon the belief that it is a god and an object of worship.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 90:

The Most High said: ﴿And Harun had already said to them before: "O my people, you are only being tested by it."﴾ That is: you are being tried by it.

﴿And indeed your Lord is the Most Merciful﴾ That is: your worshipped one is the Most Merciful, not what you have taken as a deity.

And His words: ﴿So follow me﴾ That is: follow me in the worship of God. ﴿And obey my command﴾ in abandoning the worship of the calf.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 91:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said: "We will not cease to be devoted to it (the calf) until Moses returns to us."﴾ That is: we will not cease to remain persistent in its worship, ﴿until Moses returns to us﴾.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verses 92–93:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "O Harun..."﴾ There is an implied elision here, namely that Musa turned back and said, "O Harun."

And His saying: ﴿"What prevented you, when you saw them going astray, from following me? Have you then disobeyed my command?"﴾ The particle "la" (lā) is extra (zā'idah), and its meaning is: "that you follow me."

And His saying: ﴿"Have you then disobeyed my command?"﴾ means: "Have you opposed my command?"

If someone says: Do you hold that Harun opposed Musa in what Musa had asked of him, and that he was lax (dahana) toward the worshippers of the calf and did not strictly prohibit them from it? The answer: Musa had only asked Harun to take his place among his people and to be gentle with them. Harun judged that he should not fight them, and that refraining from fighting them was the better course. Musa judged that he should fight them, and judged that fighting was the better course. This is the opinion of one mujtahid differing from the opinion of another mujtahid, and there is no fault in it. Musa only rebuked him for leaving off fighting, meaning: "If I had been in your place, I would have fought them, so why did you not do the same?"

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verses 92–93:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "O Harun..."﴾ There is an implied elision here, namely that Musa turned back and said, "O Harun."

And His saying: ﴿"What prevented you, when you saw them going astray, from following me? Have you then disobeyed my command?"﴾ The particle "la" (lā) is extra (zā'idah), and its meaning is: "that you follow me."

And His saying: ﴿"Have you then disobeyed my command?"﴾ means: "Have you opposed my command?"

If someone says: Do you hold that Harun opposed Musa in what Musa had asked of him, and that he was lax (dahana) toward the worshippers of the calf and did not strictly prohibit them from it? The answer: Musa had only asked Harun to take his place among his people and to be gentle with them. Harun judged that he should not fight them, and that refraining from fighting them was the better course. Musa judged that he should fight them, and judged that fighting was the better course. This is the opinion of one mujtahid differing from the opinion of another mujtahid, and there is no fault in it. Musa only rebuked him for leaving off fighting, meaning: "If I had been in your place, I would have fought them, so why did you not do the same?"

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 94:

The Exalted's statement: ﴿He said, "O son of my mother"﴾. It was recited as "Yā ibna umm" with a fatha (naṣb) and as "Yābna umm" with a kasra. This has been explained before.

And His statement: ﴿Do not seize me by my beard nor by my head﴾. Ibn ʿAbbās said: he seized his head with his right hand and seized his beard with his left. It is also said that the intended meaning of "the head" is the hair of the head. It is also said that by "the head" he meant the ear. If someone says: this is a display of contempt toward one of the prophets of God, and so it would be a grave sin (kabīrah, major sin), how then could Moses have done this? The answer: it is possible that such an act was not a sign of contempt in their custom, so seizing by the beard was, among them, like seizing by the palm. Some of them said: he seized his brother's beard the way a person takes hold of his own beard when angry, thereby treating him as himself. It has been narrated that ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, when he became angry, would twist his moustache. The best of the answers is that this was the act of a person toward one like him and of his kind when angry, so it is a minor sin (ṣaghīrah), not a major one, and minor sins are permissible for the prophets. The reason he said "mother" and did not mention "father" was to soften his heart toward himself.

And His statement: ﴿Indeed, I feared that you would say, "You have caused a division among the Children of Israel"﴾. This explains what he had judged as an opinion: he feared that you would say, "You made them into factions: one faction worshipped the calf, one faction fought, and one faction held back from fighting, and it became unclear to them whether fighting was permissible or not, and another faction denied it, so why did they not fight?" All of this division would have been permissible had Aaron fought.

And His statement: ﴿And you did not observe my word﴾, i.e., you did not preserve my word. This refers to His statement: ﴿Take my place among my people and set things right﴾ (and it has been explained that the meaning of "and set things right" is "be gentle"), so he judged that gentleness was for him to restrain his hand.

God's words, "He said: 'What then is your affair, O Samiri?'" The people of exegesis said: When Harun had offered the excuse he offered, Musa turned to the Samiri and said, "What is your affair, O Samiri?" Al-khatb (the great matter, the grave affair) is the weighty matter from among affairs. The meaning of the verse is: What is this grave matter that you have brought?

And His saying: ﴿He said: I perceived what they did not perceive﴾. I saw what they did not see. It is also said: I understood what they did not understand.

And His saying: ﴿So I grasped a handful from the trace of the Messenger﴾. The well-known reading is with the dotted ḍād (ض). Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī read فقبصت with the undotted ṣād (ص). The difference between them is that al-qabḍ (grasping) is taking with the full palm, while al-qabṣ is taking with the tips of the fingers.

And His saying: ﴿from the trace of the Messenger﴾ means: from the dust of the hoof of Jibrīl's horse. If someone asks: how did he know this, and how did he see Jibrīl among all the people? The answer to this is in two respects. The first: when his mother gave birth to him in the year in which the prophets were being killed, she placed him in a cave out of fear for him. Then God sent Jibrīl to raise and nourish him, because God had decreed through his hand the trial that was to come. When he saw him, he recognised him and took the dust. The second respect: Jibrīl was on a dappled white stallion, and that horse was called the horse of life. Whenever the horse placed its hoof on a place, whatever was beneath its hoof became green. So he knew that it was the horse of life. He had heard of it, and that the one upon whom Jibrīl was riding was [the Messenger]. So he took the handful.

And His saying: ﴿So I threw it﴾ means: I cast it into the mouth of the calf. Some of them have said: this is why the calf lowed, because the dust had been taken from beneath the horse of life.

And His saying: ﴿And thus my self enticed me﴾ means: my self made it seem fair to me.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 97:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Go, for you have in this life that you will say, "No touching."﴾ That is: "No touching, no touching." In the narrative: Musa invoked a curse upon him, so he began to wander with the wild beasts. It is also related that whenever he touched anyone or anyone touched him, both of them would become feverish. The poet said: "Tamim are like the people (rahṭ) of the Samiri, and his saying: 'Surely the Samiri does not want any touching (mas\u0101s)'."

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: The Samiri was a man from the people of Kirman, and it is said: from Bajarma. Most scholars say that he was from the Children of Israel, from a group (rahṭ) called the Samiriyya.

His saying: ﴿And there is for you an appointment you will not fail to meet.﴾ That is: you will not be able to deny it. Its meaning is that God will recompense you for your deed and you will not escape Him. It was also recited as "lan tukhlafahu" with a kasra on the lam, meaning: you will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection for the appointed punishment, and you will not be absent from it.

His saying: ﴿And look at your god to which you were devoted, remaining at it.﴾ That is: you continued to remain devoted to it.

His saying: ﴿We will surely burn it﴾. It was also recited as "lanuhriqannahu" from burning (al-ihraq), and both have the same meaning, which is burning with fire. It is related from Ali and Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that they recited "lanuhriqannahu" and this is the reading of Abu Ja'far. Its meaning is: "We will surely file it down with a file (mibrad)." In the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "We will surely slaughter it, then we will surely burn it."

His saying: ﴿Then we will surely scatter it into the sea, scattering.﴾ That is: we will disperse it into the sea, dispersing it.

The Exalted's saying: ﴿Your God is only Allah, other than whom there is no god, He has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾. That is: His knowledge encompasses everything. And they said: this is among the eloquent expressions of the Qur'an.

Almighty Allah's saying: ﴿Thus do We relate to you some of the news of what has already passed﴾, i.e., the reports of those who came before.

And His saying: ﴿And We have certainly given you from Us a reminder﴾. The "reminder" (dhikr) here is: the Qur'an.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 100:

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿Whoever turns away from it﴾, i.e., from the Qur'an.

And His statement: ﴿indeed he will bear on the Day of Resurrection a burden﴾, i.e., a weight, and its meaning: a sin that weighs him down.

Their saying: ﴿abiding therein﴾, meaning: remaining in the punishment of the burden (of sin).
